strengths: Rigorous and complete mathematical treatment: the real-analyticity framework, measure-zero collision argument (Theorem 2.2), and the absolute-continuity preservation under GD (Theorem 2.3 / Appendix C) are carefully worked out with full formal proofs, including a nontrivial witness construction and a Hessian-spectrum analysis to show the GD Jacobian is nondegenerate a.e.

A genuine delta over the closest prior work (Sutter et al., 2025): the paper proves injectivity at the operationally relevant last-token state (not just the full hidden-state matrix) and, crucially, shows injectivity survives training, which prior work did not address.

The paper does not stop at theory: SIPIT operationalizes the result with a provable O(T·|V|) exact-recovery guarantee, robustness analysis (margin-based tolerance ε), and strong empirical results (100% exact recovery, ~100x faster than brute force).

Extensive empirical validation: ~5 billion pairwise comparisons, an exhaustive 343-billion-pair stress test, across six model families (GPT-2, Gemma-3, Llama-3.1, Mistral, Phi-4, TinyStories) and all layers, consistently showing separations far above threshold.

Clear positioning and honest discussion of failure cases (e.g., tied embeddings break injectivity), thoughtful implications for privacy/regulation, and a solid reproducibility statement with anonymized code.
Well-organized appendix that is self-contained, from vectorization lemmas to the change-of-variables machinery, making the proofs verifiable.
weaknesses: The headline result is less surprising than framed: with continuously random embeddings and a finite vocabulary, injectivity of the discrete-to-continuous map is a fairly expected genericity statement, and the core tools (analytic zero sets, IFT, pushforward of absolutely continuous measures) are standard. The intellectual novelty is incremental relative to Sutter et al. (2025), essentially extending the same machinery to the last-token state and to finite GD horizons.

Theory–practice gap: the training-preservation theorem covers only GD/mini-batch SGD with step sizes in (0,1) on an analytic cross-entropy loss, while all experimental models were trained with Adam and, in several cases (e.g., Gemma), use tied embeddings, quantization, or other non-analytic components that the paper itself acknowledges break injectivity. The theorem therefore does not strictly apply to the models tested; the empirical results compensate, but the claims of 'guaranteed' injectivity in practical pipelines are stronger than the formal coverage.

The algorithmic contribution is modest: given causal masking and one-step injectivity, sequential token-by-token enumeration (with optional gradient guidance) is a fairly direct and predictable construction; the 'linear-time' claim is O(T·|V|) verifier tests each requiring forward passes, so the constant factors are large.

Evaluation of SIPIT is limited to GPT-2 Small on 100 prompts of 20 tokens; there is no inversion experiment on larger/modern models (collision tests only), leaving scalability of the recovery method underexplored.

Baselines are thin: the main comparison (HardPrompts, adapted by the authors from a vision-language method) achieves 0.00 accuracy, and other inversion methods are declared 'not directly comparable' rather than adapted; the 'collision threshold' of 1e-6 is heuristic and not justified w.r.t. floating-point precision.

Presentation: the main text is repetitive and somewhat over-claims ('first algorithm', 'fundamental property'), and the appendix invests many pages proving elementary facts (exponential is analytic, etc.), inflating length without adding substance.

Significance is real but bounded: white-box access to hidden states plus full model parameters is a strong threat model already known to leak text (Morris et al., 2023a); the added value is exactness and guarantees rather than a new attack capability.

strengths: The paper is clearly written and well-organized, with complete formal proofs provided in an extensive appendix (real-analyticity of Transformer components, measure-zero collision sets, preservation of absolute continuity under gradient descent).

The core mathematical argument (real-analytic functions have measure-zero zero sets unless identically zero, plus explicit witness constructions) is correct and carefully executed, including the Inverse Function Theorem / countable chart cover argument for GD steps.
The empirical collision searches (billions of pairwise comparisons across six models, exhaustive continuation tests) are thorough and well-suited to verifying the theory empirically.
The discussion of privacy/regulatory implications of recoverable hidden states is a genuinely interesting angle and connects the technical result to real deployment concerns.
The paper is honest about failure cases (tied embeddings, quantization) and positions itself carefully relative to Sutter et al. (2025) and Morris et al. (2023).
weaknesses: Limited novelty of the central theoretical result. The claim that a fixed finite set of discrete inputs maps injectively into R^d for almost all parameters of a smooth parametric family is a near-trivial genericity argument that applies to essentially any sufficiently expressive smooth model, not specifically to Transformers. The increment over Sutter et al. (2025), who already prove almost-sure injectivity of Transformers at initialization, is incremental: differing at the last-token state and extending to finitely many GD steps, which is a fairly direct consequence of standard pushforward/absolute-continuity arguments.

The 'provable linear-time guarantee' of SIPIT is oversold. The worst-case O(T|V|) bound is a trivial property of the algorithm's construction (it simply enumerates the vocabulary per position with early stopping), not a nontrivial algorithmic contribution. Correctness of the sequential matching procedure is immediate given injectivity, so Theorem 3.1 adds little beyond Theorem 2.3.

The experimental inversion setting is much easier than the framing suggests. With white-box access to full hidden-state matrices at a layer (including the residual stream and, at shallow layers, essentially the input embeddings themselves), exact recovery is nearly trivial, echoing known results (Morris et al., 2023a) that embeddings reveal the text. The baselines are weak: HARDPROMPTS was designed for a different objective and had to be heavily adapted, and BRUTEFORCE is just an ablation of the proposed method; no comparison to trained inverters or logprob-based inversion is possible under their own positioning.

Practical significance is questionable: the measure-zero guarantee says nothing about near-collisions, quantization, or noisy/low-precision hidden states — precisely the conditions under which inversion methods operate in practice. The gap between 'almost-sure injectivity in exact arithmetic' and 'usable invertibility' is acknowledged only briefly and left as future work.

The claim of being 'the first algorithm to provably and efficiently reconstruct exact input from hidden activations' overstates the contribution given how straightforward greedy prefix-wise matching is once causality and injectivity are established, and given prior work on text recovery from embeddings/logits.

Significance for the community is modest: the main conceptual takeaway (hidden states essentially encode the prompt) is already widely appreciated from the embedding-inversion literature, and the formal result does not change how models are analyzed, trained, or deployed in a concrete way.

Some assumptions deserve more scrutiny for the models actually tested: the theory assumes real-analytic activations and untied embeddings with learned absolute positional encodings, while modern architectures (RMSNorm, SwiGLU variants, RoPE, tied embeddings in some models) require adaptations that are only briefly addressed; the gap between the formal model of Appendix B and the deployed models in Section 4 is not fully closed.

strengths: The paper is technically careful and rigorous: the real-analyticity framework (Theorem 2.1), the witness-based proof that collision sets are measure zero (Theorem 2.2), and the pushforward/absolute-continuity argument that gradient descent does not create collisions (Theorem 2.3) are all coherent, and the appendices provide complete, self-contained proofs including explicit witness constructions.

There is a genuine, well-identified delta over prior work: Sutter et al. (2025) establish injectivity of the full hidden-state matrix only at initialization, whereas this paper proves injectivity of the operationally relevant last-token state and shows it is preserved under (finite-horizon) gradient descent, including SGD/mini-batch variants.

SIPIT turns the theoretical property into a constructive, training-free exact inversion procedure with a correctness theorem (Theorem D.2) and robustness analysis via acceptance regions and margins (Proposition D.1), which is more than a heuristic demonstration.

The empirical collision studies are unusually thorough for this kind of claim: ~5 billion pairwise comparisons across six models and many layers, plus an exhaustive continuation search (343B pairs) on the closest prefix prompts, consistently showing separations orders of magnitude above threshold.

The 100% exact prompt recovery on pre-trained models (vs. failure of HardPrompts and prohibitive brute-force cost) is a compelling practical result, and the privacy/regulatory discussion (hidden states as 'the prompt in disguise') gives the work clear real-world significance.
The paper is well positioned relative to prior inversion literature (Morris et al., Nazir et al., Zhang et al.), clearly articulating why black-box/logprob inversion is a different setting.
weaknesses: Limited conceptual depth of the main theorem: once the finite prompt set and real-analyticity are established, the 'measure-zero collision' conclusion is a fairly standard application of the analytic zero-set theorem, and the a.s. injectivity of a random smooth map on a finite domain is close to expected. The theorem is correct but the framing ('replace a long-assumed property with a rigorous theorem') somewhat oversells a modest mathematical observation.

The almost-sure guarantee is qualitatively weak: it gives no quantitative lower bound on separation margins, which are the quantity that actually matters for stable inversion. Margins are only studied empirically; a gap between the theory (positive a.s.) and practice (unknown, possibly tiny margins) remains unaddressed.

The theory does not cover several components of the very models tested: weight tying (explicitly acknowledged to break the result, yet GPT-2 ties embeddings), quantized/low-precision weights, and modern optimizers (Adam, momentum) beyond vanilla GD/SGD with step sizes in (0,1). The claimed applicability to 'six state-of-the-art language models' is thus looser than the formal setting.

The 'linear-time guarantee' for SIPIT is somewhat misleading: the worst-case bound is Theta(T|V|) verifier tests, each requiring a forward pass, which is essentially exhaustive search complexity; the actual contribution is the gradient-guided policy improving the constant/practical cost. Comparing SIPIT against its own no-policy ablation makes the headline speedup partly self-referential.

Inversion experiments are limited to GPT-2 Small, 100 prompts of 20 tokens, on a single GPU. Demonstrating exact recovery on larger models (Llama-3.1-8B, Mistral-7B are used only for the collision tests) would substantially strengthen the operational claims; robustness of inversion to noise is only treated theoretically.

The appendix is excessively long and padded with elementary material (proofs that exp, polynomials, softmax, matrix products are real-analytic; Bearer [REDACTED] of R^p), which dilutes the contribution and suggests the core ideas are thin relative to the page count.

Some proof sketches contain minor sloppiness (e.g., the claim in Theorem C.2's Case A that an all-zero-parameter network 'acts as the identity' ignores the LayerNorm, though the conclusion still holds), which slightly undermines confidence in the otherwise careful presentation.
